clean_story: "Fewer clicks. Clearer goals. The term interface simplicity comes from stripping a tool down to only what’s needed, like a knife with no extra blades. A screen may look empty, but every button has one job. Think of a light switch: flip up for on, down for off. No menus, no settings. This is the same logic behind the first iPod wheel—one dial to scroll, one button to select. No manuals. No confusion. In 1970, Xerox PARC’s Alto computer used overlapping windows, but its true breakthrough was the desktop metaphor: files as paper, folders as drawers. Users already knew how to organize paper. The machine just mirrored that. Today, a traffic light uses three colors because more would slow reaction time. Tests show people recognize red faster than any other hue. Interface simplicity isn’t about removing options. It’s about removing doubt. Three related subjects are user intuition, design constraints and hidden complexity."
